events.title: Animal Electricity Discovered
events.blurb: An Italian physician published a decade of experiments showing that the muscles of dead frogs could be made to contract when touched with two different metals — or when connected to a charged conductor — demonstrating that animal tissues themselves generate and respond to electrical currents. The finding launched the science of electrophysiology and inspired fierce debate about the nature of electricity and life.
events.revealBlurb: 1791 — Luigi Galvani called the phenomenon "animal electricity"; Alessandro Volta argued it was purely metallic electricity and invented the first battery to prove the point. Both were partly right. The argument inspired Mary Shelley: she attended a lecture on Galvanic reanimation and later wrote Frankenstein.

events.title: On the Origin of Species Published
events.blurb: A 502-page book argued that all species of life descended from common ancestors through a process of natural selection, where individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survived and reproduced at higher rates. The first print run of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on the day it was offered for sale.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1859 — Darwin had sat on the theory for twenty years, terrified of the controversy. He finally rushed it to press only after Alfred Russel Wallace independently wrote him a letter describing the same mechanism. The two men's papers were presented jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858.

events.title: X-Rays Discovered
events.blurb: While experimenting with cathode ray tubes in a darkened laboratory, a German physicist noticed that a fluorescent screen across the room glowed even though it was shielded from the tube's visible light. The mysterious new rays penetrated cardboard, wood, and flesh, but were blocked by dense metal. Within weeks he had produced the first medical radiograph, showing the bones of his wife's hand.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Röntgen kept the discovery secret for seven weeks, repeating every experiment before telling anyone. He named the rays "X" because he didn't know what they were. He won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and donated the prize money to his university.

events.title: General Relativity Confirmed by Eclipse
events.blurb: Two British expeditions sent to observe a total solar eclipse measured the positions of stars near the Sun's edge and found their apparent positions had shifted by an amount predicted by a new theory of gravitation — confirming that massive objects warp the fabric of space itself. The results overturned the classical picture of gravity as a force acting at a distance and made the paper's author internationally famous overnight.
events.revealBlurb: November 6, 1919 — Arthur Eddington announced the results to a packed joint meeting of the Royal Society and Royal Astronomical Society in London. The Times headline read "Revolution in Science." Some later scholars questioned the data quality, but multiple subsequent eclipses fully confirmed the result.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: Executive Order 8802
events.blurb: Facing a threatened mass march on Washington organized by a prominent Black labor leader, a U.S. president signed an executive order banning racial discrimination in the defense industry and federal government. It was the first federal action against employment discrimination since Reconstruction. The threatened march was called off; the larger March would come 22 years later.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1941 — Franklin Roosevelt, pushed by A. Philip Randolph. Randolph had assembled 100,000 marchers and refused to call it off without the order. The order created the Fair Employment Practice Committee — a template for later civil rights enforcement.

events.title: Little Rock Nine
events.blurb: Nine Black teenagers, escorted by federal troops, walked through the front doors of an Arkansas capital's previously all-white high school, three weeks after the governor had called out the National Guard to bar them. The images of the 101st Airborne at the schoolhouse door — bayonets fixed — broadcast on the nightly news forced a hostile public to confront massive resistance.
events.revealBlurb: September 25, 1957 — Central High School, Little Rock. President Eisenhower federalized the entire Arkansas National Guard to override Governor Orval Faubus. One of the nine, Elizabeth Eckford, was famously photographed walking alone through a screaming mob on an earlier attempt.

events.title: Black Panther Party Founded
events.blurb: Two community-college students in a California Bay Area city drafted a ten-point program demanding full employment, decent housing, exemption from military service, and an end to police brutality for Black Americans. They organized armed neighborhood patrols to monitor police, opened free-breakfast programs for children, and ran medical clinics. The FBI declared them "the greatest threat to internal security" within four years.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 1966 — Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland. J. Edgar Hoover's COINTELPRO infiltrated the party and fabricated rivalries between it and the US Organization; the free breakfasts, which he called "the greatest threat," fed 20,000 children a day at their peak.

events.title: MLK Day Signed
events.blurb: After 15 years of advocacy by civil rights leaders, Congress passed and the president signed legislation establishing the third Monday of January as a federal holiday honoring the slain civil rights leader. The fight to pass it had drawn bitter opposition from some senators, including one who conducted a 16-day filibuster. It became the first federal holiday commemorating an African-American.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 1983 — Ronald Reagan. Arizona voters rejected recognizing the holiday in 1990; the NFL moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Phoenix in response, and the state reversed course. New Hampshire, the last holdout, adopted it in 1999.

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: First Animal in Earth Orbit
events.blurb: A stray mixed-breed dog named Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, a 508 kg spacecraft with no reentry capability. Laika survived liftoff and initial orbit but died from overheating within five to seven hours when a thermal regulation system failed — a fact withheld from the public for decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1957 — Sputnik 2. The Soviets announced Laika died painlessly after several days; the truth wasn't confirmed until 2002. The spacecraft had been built in under four weeks on Khrushchev's orders to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. Laika has since been honored with a monument in Moscow and a postage stamp in more than 70 countries.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: ISS First Crewed Occupation
events.blurb: A three-person crew docked a Soyuz capsule to the International Space Station's Zvezda module at 09:21 UTC, beginning a continuous human presence in low Earth orbit that has not been interrupted since. The station at that point consisted of three connected modules spanning roughly 27 meters, a fraction of its eventual 109-meter length.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 2000 — Expedition 1. Commander Bill Shepherd radioed NASA to request the station's call sign be changed from "Alpha" to "International Space Station" — a small act of diplomacy that stuck. The crew of two Russians and one American had access to less than 425 cubic meters of living space, about the volume of a large school bus.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Water Confirmed on the Moon
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe detected spectral signatures consistent with water molecules during its 25-minute controlled descent to the lunar south pole, with readings from a mass spectrometer increasing steadily as the probe flew toward higher latitudes. Three instruments on the orbiting spacecraft corroborated the finding, confirming that water ice is present across the lunar surface.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 2008 — Chandrayaan-1/MIP. The probe was decorated with the Indian national flag and crashed intentionally near Shackleton Crater at 85° south — making India the fourth nation to place an object on the Moon. The water discovery reversed decades of scientific consensus that the Moon was bone dry, reshaping plans for every future lunar base concept.

events.title: Nightingale at Scutari
events.blurb: A 34-year-old British nurse arrived with 38 volunteer nurses at a filthy military hospital in a former Turkish barracks outside a Bosphorus capital, where British wounded from a Crimean war were dying of typhus, cholera, and dysentery at far higher rates than from combat wounds. Her reforms — sanitation, proper food, hand-washing, laundry — cut the death rate from 42 percent to 2 percent in six months. Her subsequent statistical advocacy reshaped nursing as a profession.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1854 — Florence Nightingale at Scutari (now Üsküdar, Istanbul). Her nighttime rounds with an oil lamp produced the "Lady with the Lamp" sobriquet. She returned to London with chronic brucellosis, spent most of the rest of her life bedridden, and still wrote 200 books and reports. She lived to 90.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine
events.blurb: A 62-year-old French chemist, who had been working for years on vaccines against animal diseases, administered his experimental rabies vaccine — desiccated spinal cord tissue from infected rabbits — to a 9-year-old Alsatian boy who had been savaged by a rabid dog two days earlier. The boy received 13 injections over ten days and survived. Rabies, previously universally fatal once symptoms appeared, now had an effective post-exposure prophylaxis.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1885 — Louis Pasteur; patient was Joseph Meister. Pasteur was not licensed as a physician; he could have been prosecuted if the boy had died. Meister grew up, became the gatekeeper at the Institut Pasteur, and is said to have killed himself in 1940 rather than let Nazi troops enter Pasteur's tomb (disputed; he may have died from gas poisoning unrelated).

events.title: Röntgen Discovers X-Rays
events.blurb: A 50-year-old German physicist, working with a cathode-ray tube covered in black cardboard, noticed that a paper screen coated in barium platinocyanide glowed even when placed some distance away. He realized the tube was emitting an invisible, unknown type of radiation. Further experiments showed the rays penetrated paper, wood, aluminum, and even human flesh — but not bone. He published an image of his wife's hand, showing her skeleton and wedding ring.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen at the University of Würzburg. He called the phenomenon "X" rays because he didn't know what they were. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. The image of his wife's hand, published in early 1896, is arguably the first diagnostic X-ray.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: HPV Vaccine Approved
events.blurb: A quadrivalent vaccine against human papillomavirus — the cause of virtually all cervical cancers and several other cancers — received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration for girls and women aged 9-26. The vaccine, developed initially by an Australian immunologist and colleagues, had been shown in clinical trials to be nearly 100 percent effective at preventing infection by the viral strains responsible for 70 percent of cervical cancer. Cervical cancer incidence began declining visibly within a decade.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 2006 — Gardasil (Merck), developed from research by Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou. Australia's school-based vaccination program has since essentially eliminated cervical-cancer-causing HPV strains from young women there. The vaccine's politically fraught rollout in the US slowed uptake in the 2010s.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Bangladesh Liberation War
events.blurb: Pakistan's army launched a crackdown on the Bengali-speaking eastern wing of its own country, displacing an estimated 10 million refugees across the border into India. India intervened militarily; within thirteen days it had driven the Pakistani army to capitulate in a Bengali capital, where 93,000 surrendered in the largest military surrender since WWII. A new nation was born.
events.revealBlurb: December 3-16, 1971 — victory at the Instrument of Surrender at Ramna Race Course, Dhaka. Bangladesh Liberation Day is December 16. Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw commanded the Indian effort; Lt. General A.A.K. Niazi signed the surrender.

events.title: Indira Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: The prime minister, walking from her bungalow to a garden office for a scheduled interview with a British filmmaker, was shot 31 times at close range by two of her own Sikh bodyguards. She was rushed to a nearby hospital and died during surgery. Four days of anti-Sikh riots followed in the capital, organized partly by politicians of her own party, killing at least 3,000 people. Her son Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister the same evening.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1984 — Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, bodyguards who had both been retained despite security concerns after Blue Star. The Justice Nanavati Commission documented the organized nature of the subsequent riots; convictions have come only in the last few years.

events.title: Economic Liberalization
events.blurb: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis so acute that the country had airlifted 47 tonnes of its gold reserves to London as collateral, a new finance minister presented a budget that systematically dismantled the license-permit-quota economy that had governed Indian business for four decades. Industrial licensing was abolished, imports liberalized, foreign investment welcomed. The economy would nearly quintuple over the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1991 — Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget speech. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao provided the political cover. Singh, invoking Victor Hugo, declared: "No power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come."

events.title: Demonetisation
events.blurb: In a surprise eight-o'clock television address, the prime minister announced that the two largest-denomination banknotes in circulation — 86 percent of all currency by value — would cease to be legal tender at midnight. The stated targets were counterfeit money, black money, and terrorism financing. Long queues formed outside banks for weeks; small businesses and day-labourers, most paid in cash, were disproportionately hit. Subsequent data showed most demonetised cash returned to the banking system.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2016 — Narendra Modi. By the Reserve Bank's own accounting, 99.3 percent of the old notes were eventually exchanged. Counterfeit detection was negligible. The policy's effect on corruption is still debated; its effect on GDP was negative.

events.title: The Tale of Genji
events.blurb: A Japanese noblewoman serving at the imperial court of a Heian-era empress completed a 54-chapter prose narrative following the life, loves, and political career of a fictional son of an emperor. Full of psychological interiority, metaphorical poetry, and a sophisticated unreliable narrator, it is widely regarded as the world's first modern novel. It was written over more than a decade and circulated in manuscript among the court.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1010 CE — Murasaki Shikibu. The earliest surviving complete manuscript dates from the 13th century. It has been translated into English several times; Arthur Waley's 1925-33 version introduced it to the West, but recent translations are preferred for accuracy.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Shakespeare's First Folio
events.blurb: Seven years after the Stratford-born playwright's death, two of his fellow actors compiled and published a folio edition of 36 of his plays — 18 of which had never been printed before. Without the volume, half the plays, including Macbeth, Julius Caesar, and The Tempest, would have been lost. 750 copies were printed; 235 are known to survive today, fetching tens of millions at auction.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1623 — compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell. It was sold for £1 — roughly £200 today. A recently discovered copy was unmasked at a Scottish library in 2016. The folio standardized the canonical text of most of the plays.

events.title: Things Fall Apart Published
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Nigerian broadcaster published a short novel tracing the life of an Igbo wrestler and farmer in a southeastern Nigerian village and the arrival of English colonial missionaries that destroys his world. Written in English deliberately infused with Igbo idiom, the book pushed back against European literary stereotypes of African societies. It has since been translated into 50 languages and sold over 20 million copies — the most widely read book by any African author.
events.revealBlurb: 1958 — Chinua Achebe. Its title is from Yeats's poem "The Second Coming." Achebe later famously accused Joseph Conrad of racism in "Heart of Darkness." He was in a serious car crash in 1990 that left him paralyzed from the waist down; he continued writing for over two more decades.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: Jeannette Rankin Elected to Congress
events.blurb: A 36-year-old social worker and suffrage organizer from a western U.S. state was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives, becoming the first woman to hold federal office in the country. She took office four years before women nationally could vote. She would vote against entering both world wars — the only member of Congress to do so twice.
events.revealBlurb: November 7, 1916 — Montana had given women the state vote in 1914. Rankin's 1941 "no" vote on the declaration of war against Japan made her a pariah; she had to be escorted to her office by the Capitol police. "As a woman I can't go to war," she said, "and I refuse to send anyone else."

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Benazir Bhutto Becomes PM
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Oxford and Harvard educated politician whose father had been hanged by a previous military government was sworn in as prime minister of a large South Asian Muslim-majority country, becoming the first woman to head the government of any Muslim-majority state. Her ruling coalition was fragile; she would be dismissed twice on corruption charges and would be assassinated 19 years later while campaigning for a third term.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1988 — Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan. She was assassinated in Rawalpindi on December 27, 2007, after a campaign rally. Her 19-year-old son Bilawal was named co-chair of her party within days.

events.title: Ruth Bader Ginsburg Confirmed
events.blurb: A 60-year-old federal appeals court judge, a former ACLU lawyer who had successfully argued six of the era's most important gender-discrimination cases before the court she was now joining, was confirmed 96-3 as the second woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court. She would serve 27 years, becoming — somewhat unexpectedly for a cautious litigator — a late-life pop-culture icon on the Court's liberal wing.
events.revealBlurb: August 10, 1993 — nominated by Bill Clinton. She acquired the nickname "Notorious RBG" from a law student's Tumblr in 2013. She died September 18, 2020, enabling the confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett eight days before the presidential election.

events.title: Great Lisbon Earthquake
events.blurb: On the morning of a major Catholic holy day, a magnitude-9 earthquake struck off the Atlantic coast of a European capital while most residents were at Mass. The quake was followed within 40 minutes by a tsunami that rolled up the Tagus River, and a citywide fire that burned for five days. Roughly 40,000 of the city's 200,000 inhabitants died.
events.revealBlurb: November 1, 1755 — All Saints' Day in Lisbon. Voltaire wrote his anti-optimist poem about it, then Candide. The Portuguese prime minister, the Marquis of Pombal, supposedly asked "What now? We bury the dead and feed the living" and rebuilt the city on a grid.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Bhola Cyclone
events.blurb: A tropical cyclone with 185 km/h winds made landfall on the low-lying islands of the Bay of Bengal delta at high tide, driving a 10-metre storm surge over villages built at sea level. At least 300,000 people died, possibly up to 500,000 — the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history. The East Pakistan government's slow response fueled the separatist movement that led to war within months.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1970 — East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). The relief failure helped trigger the Bangladesh Liberation War the following March. The former Beatle George Harrison organized the Concert for Bangladesh to raise funds.

events.title: Bhopal Disaster
events.blurb: A cloud of methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a pesticide plant on the outskirts of a central Indian city shortly after midnight, drifting over densely populated slums whose inhabitants woke choking and blind. Between 8,000 and 16,000 people died in the immediate aftermath; 500,000 were injured. Groundwater at the site remains contaminated four decades on.
events.revealBlurb: December 2-3, 1984 — Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. The plant was owned by Union Carbide; the American parent company settled for $470 million, a fraction of the actual cost. The CEO, Warren Anderson, was briefly arrested and then quietly released; India's extradition requests were ignored.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: Truman Doctrine
events.blurb: Addressing a joint session of Congress, a U.S. president requested $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey and announced a sweeping new foreign policy: the United States would support "free peoples" resisting armed minorities or outside pressures. The speech committed America to global containment of communism.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1947 — Harry Truman needed just 18 minutes. Behind the rhetoric: Britain, bankrupted by war, had quietly told Washington it could no longer prop up the Greek government. America stepped into the imperial vacuum.

events.title: Korean War Armistice
events.blurb: After three years and more than two million deaths, military commanders from three nations signed a ceasefire in a frontier village, establishing a 4-kilometre-wide demilitarized strip along the 38th parallel where fighting had essentially started. No peace treaty has ever been signed. The two Koreas remain technically at war.
events.revealBlurb: July 27, 1953 — signed at Panmunjom. The DMZ is now the most heavily mined place on Earth. Because no peace treaty followed, a single gunshot across the line could theoretically restart the war tomorrow.

events.title: Khrushchev Secret Speech
events.blurb: Speaking to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party's 20th Congress, a new premier delivered a four-hour denunciation of his predecessor's personality cult, show trials, and mass purges. The text was supposed to remain secret but leaked within months, shattering communist movements worldwide and launching a partial cultural thaw at home.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1956 — Nikita Khrushchev, three years after Stalin's death. A Polish journalist smuggled the text to Israeli intelligence, who gave it to the CIA. Millions of Soviet prisoners were rehabilitated in the following years.

events.title: Berlin Wall Falls
events.blurb: An East German government spokesman announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border immediately, triggering jubilant crowds who arrived at checkpoints and began dismantling the 155-kilometre concrete barrier with hammers and their bare hands. More than two million East Germans crossed into West Berlin during the following weekend alone.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.blurb: An East German spokesman, reading hastily from a note and misunderstanding its contents, announced at a televised press conference that new travel rules would take effect "immediately." Within hours, tens of thousands of jubilant East Berliners massed at the crossings. Confused border guards, receiving no clear orders, simply let them through. People scrambled onto the concrete barrier with hammers.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 1989 — the spokesman was Günter Schabowski, who had skimmed the briefing note just before the press conference. Asked when the rules took effect, he shrugged: "As far as I know — immediately." The wall, built in a single night 28 years earlier, came down in a single night too.

events.title: UNIVAC Predicts Election
events.blurb: A televised presidential election broadcast featured, as a novelty, a commercial digital computer that had been sold to the Census Bureau six months earlier. Fed early returns by its operators, the machine predicted an Eisenhower landslide hours before conventional forecasters were willing to call the race. CBS' broadcasters initially didn't trust it and understated its projection on-air. The machine was right.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1952 — UNIVAC I, on CBS. The machine predicted 438 electoral votes for Eisenhower; the actual result was 442. After the election, CBS' on-air introducer Charles Collingwood admitted they had held back UNIVAC's early call for fear it would look ridiculous.

events.title: Intel 4004 Microprocessor Released
events.blurb: Intel released a 4-bit central processing unit containing 2,300 transistors on a silicon chip the size of a fingernail, capable of 60,000 operations per second. Originally designed for a Japanese calculator company, it became the world's first commercially available microprocessor — the prototype for every CPU that followed.

events.title: Apple II Released
events.blurb: A young Californian computer company released their second machine — and the first mass-market personal computer designed for non-hobbyists, with built-in color graphics, a working keyboard, a plastic case, and the ability to display text and graphics simultaneously. It shipped for $1,298 and found a broad market among small businesses, schools, and households. Apple's revenues grew 700 percent a year for five consecutive years.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1977 — Apple Computer. Engineered largely by Steve Wozniak. The arrival of VisiCalc two years later made it the first computer that small businesses felt they had to buy. Apple sold over 5 million Apple IIs before discontinuing the line in 1993.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Lady Gaga's Meat Dress
events.blurb: A 24-year-old American pop singer arrived at a New York awards show wearing an outfit made from 50 pounds of raw Argentine beef — flank steak fashioned into a sleeveless dress, a matching hat, a handbag, and shoes. She told a late-night host the ensemble was a protest against a military policy excluding openly gay service members. PETA criticized it; steak prices nationwide did not apparently change. The dress was later preserved as beef jerky and displayed at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 2010 — Lady Gaga (Stefani Germanotta) at the MTV VMAs. Designer Franc Fernandez. The dress won her five VMAs that night, including Video of the Year for "Bad Romance." It is now permanently on display in Cleveland.

events.title: Kim Kardashian "Breaks the Internet"
events.blurb: A 34-year-old reality TV star and entrepreneur appeared on the cover of a magazine nude, balancing a champagne glass on her bared posterior, with a headline directly daring the internet to be broken by it. The cover image was shared widely enough that the magazine's website crashed for short periods. The photograph — shot by a French photographer who had staged similar images four decades earlier — launched weeks of commentary about sexuality, race, body image, and the limits of viral marketing.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 2014 — Kim Kardashian on Paper magazine. Photographer Jean-Paul Goude had shot nearly identical images with other models in the 1970s and 80s, drawing accusations that he specifically emphasized and sexualized Black bodies. The cover did, in fact, briefly break the magazine's website.

events.title: Avengers: Endgame Opens
events.blurb: The 22nd film in a 11-year sprawling superhero cinematic universe opened in theatres worldwide, bringing together nearly every hero introduced across the previous decade for a time-travel battle against a cosmic villain. The three-hour film made $1.2 billion in its opening weekend alone — by a comfortable margin, the largest opening in box-office history — and eventually surpassed Avatar's decade-old record for highest-grossing film of all time. It marked the end of an "Infinity Saga" and the conclusion of multiple central characters' arcs.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 2019 — Avengers: Endgame from Marvel Studios. Final box office: $2.798 billion. The film required some 2,500 visual effects shots; about 90 percent of what appears on screen is CGI. Robert Downey Jr.'s Iron Man had kicked off the Marvel Cinematic Universe 11 years earlier.

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
events.blurb: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the proposed Constitution, providing the three-fourths supermajority required to bring the new framework of government into effect and replace the faltering Articles of Confederation. The document created a federal republic with three separated branches of power — a design that had no exact precedent in world history.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1788 — New Hampshire. Rhode Island didn't ratify until May 1790 — over a year after the government had already begun operating. North Carolina waited until November 1789, after the First Congress had already convened.

events.title: Gettysburg Address Delivered
events.blurb: At the dedication of a military cemetery on the grounds of the bloodiest battle of the war, Abraham Lincoln delivered a 272-word speech that redefined the purpose of the conflict — not merely preserving the Union, but completing the "unfinished work" of the Declaration of Independence by ensuring that a government of the people would not perish. Lincoln spoke for less than two minutes; the main orator that day delivered a two-hour speech that nobody remembers.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1863 — Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The battle four months earlier killed or wounded more than 50,000 men over three days. Edward Everett — the two-hour orator — wrote Lincoln privately: "I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion, in two hours, as you did in two minutes."

events.title: Pullman Strike and Federal Injunction
events.blurb: When the Pullman Company cut wages by 25 percent without reducing rents in its company-owned town south of Chicago, nearly 4,000 workers walked out that spring; within weeks, the American Railway Union's boycott of Pullman cars had paralyzed rail traffic across 29 railroads and 27 states. President Grover Cleveland dispatched federal troops and obtained a court injunction to break the strike, establishing the federal government's willingness to use military force against organized labor.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1894 — Pullman, Illinois. Eugene Debs, the ARU leader, served six months in federal prison for defying the injunction — and read socialist literature in his cell, emerging as America's most famous socialist. The strike also created Labor Day as a federal holiday, rushed through Congress as a conciliation gesture two days before Debs was arrested.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Coup of 18 Brumaire
events.blurb: A 30-year-old French artillery general, recently returned from an unsuccessful campaign in Egypt, led a coup against the five-man executive Directory that had ruled France for four years. He had political allies in the councils and military support on the ground; within two days the Directory was gone and a new three-consul system was in place with him as its dominant first consul. In name, the revolution continued. In effect, one-man rule had returned.
events.revealBlurb: November 9-10, 1799 — Napoleon Bonaparte at the Château de Saint-Cloud. He would crown himself emperor five years later. The Gregorian-calendar date in the French revolutionary calendar was 18-19 Brumaire, Year VIII.

events.title: Grito de Dolores
events.blurb: A 57-year-old Catholic priest in a rural Mexican town, learning that a conspiracy of criollo-elite revolutionaries had been uncovered, rang his church bell in the middle of the night to summon his parishioners and call for the overthrow of Spanish colonial rule. He led his ragged army of peasants and mestizos toward the capital; the colonial government crushed them within four months and he was shot. The rebellion he had started, though, continued for 11 more years.
events.revealBlurb: September 16, 1810 — Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla at Dolores, Guanajuato. The exact wording of his "grito" is not recorded. Hidalgo was captured in March 1811 and executed by firing squad on July 30, 1811. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day; the President still rings the bell each year.

events.title: Napoleon Invades Russia
events.blurb: A French emperor crossed the Neman River into Russian territory with the largest army Europe had ever seen — 680,000 men drawn from across his continental empire. His objectives were to compel Russia back into a trade embargo against Britain and to break Russian military power. The Russians fell back, burning as they withdrew, refusing pitched battle. The French reached Moscow in September to find it empty and soon burning. The retreat home through a catastrophic winter would destroy almost the entire army.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1812 — the Neman crossing. Of the 680,000 who crossed east, perhaps 40,000 returned. The retreat featured the famous crossing of the Berezina River, where improvised pontoon bridges collapsed under packed refugees; tens of thousands died in the icy water.

events.title: Revolutions of 1848
events.blurb: Political unrest that had been gathering over economic recession and demands for constitutional government erupted within weeks across most of the European continent, beginning with a winter insurrection in Paris that deposed the king. Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest, Prague, and a dozen other capitals followed within months. Liberals, nationalists, socialists, and workers briefly shared rhetoric; conservatives reorganized and, over the following year, crushed nearly every revolt. The conservative order emerged apparently reinforced — but the political grammar of 19th-century Europe had changed.
events.revealBlurb: February-June 1848 — "The Springtime of Nations." Louis-Philippe of France fled in February; Metternich resigned in Vienna in March. Only France produced lasting regime change, and it soon produced Napoleon III's Second Empire. Karl Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto that same February.

events.title: Licinian-Sextian Laws
events.blurb: After a decade of plebeian obstruction that left Rome with no consuls at all, the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus forced through three laws: one relieving debt, one limiting landholding to 500 iugera, and one requiring that at least one consul each year be a plebeian. Lucius Sextius duly became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE.
events.revealBlurb: 367 BCE, Rome. Licinius and Sextius blocked every other piece of legislation for ten straight years to force the patricians to negotiate — essentially inventing the political hostage tactic of governmental gridlock.

events.title: Spartacus Leads the Slave Revolt
events.blurb: Roughly 70 gladiators armed with kitchen knives fought their way out of a training school in Capua, seized carts of gladiatorial weapons, and retreated to the slopes of Vesuvius. Within two years their force had swelled to as many as 120,000 men, women, and children, and twice defeated consular Roman armies sent to destroy them.
events.revealBlurb: 73 BCE, Capua. Spartacus reportedly wanted to lead his followers north over the Alps to freedom; other commanders preferred to raid Italy for wealth. The disagreement split the army. After the revolt's defeat, 6,000 survivors were crucified along the 200-kilometre Appian Way.

events.title: Crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth
events.blurb: A Jewish teacher from a Galilean town, who had spent a few years preaching an apocalyptic ethical message and gathering followers, was arrested by Temple authorities in the Judean capital during a Passover festival, handed to the Roman prefect, and crucified on a charge of claiming to be "King of the Jews." He was 33. A small community of his followers, convinced he had risen from the dead three days later, carried his teachings out of Judea; within three centuries their movement was the state religion of the Roman Empire.
events.revealBlurb: c. April 3, 33 CE — Jesus of Nazareth; prefect Pontius Pilate. The precise date is debated; April 7, 30 CE is an alternative. Christianity spread slowly across the first three centuries; Emperor Constantine's 313 CE Edict of Milan ended persecution; Theodosius I made it the official Roman religion in 380 CE.

events.title: Trajan's Dacian Wars
events.blurb: Emperor Trajan led two campaigns across the Danube into Dacia — building the longest bridge the ancient world had seen — and destroyed the mountain kingdom of King Decebalus, who slit his own throat rather than be paraded through Rome. The conquest added the richest gold and silver mines in the known world to the treasury and pushed the empire to its maximum territorial extent.
events.revealBlurb: 101–106 CE. The story of both campaigns is carved in a continuous spiral 200 metres long around Trajan's Column in Rome, depicting over 2,600 figures. Trajan himself appears 58 times but is never shown fighting — he is always commanding, judging, or sacrificing.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: Final Fantasy VII Released in Japan
events.blurb: A Japanese role-playing game with pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, full orchestral-style music, and a story involving ecological collapse and corporate villainy sold out PlayStation consoles across Japan before it even launched. On release day it sold 1.75 million copies in a single country in a single day.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1997 — Final Fantasy VII launched in Japan for PlayStation. It sold 2.3 million copies in its first three days and over 6 million by 1998. Its western release September 7, 1997, introduced the JRPG genre to millions. The 2020 remake sold over 7 million copies in under four days.

events.title: Half-Life Released by Valve
events.blurb: Every first-person shooter before Half-Life presented missions as separate levels with loading screens and no coherent world. Half-Life placed the player inside a continuous unbroken environment, told its story entirely through actions the player participated in, and won more than 50 Game of the Year awards. Critics later divided gaming history into "pre-Half-Life" and "post-Half-Life" eras.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1998 — Valve's debut game released for Windows. Budgeted for lifetime sales of 180,000 copies, it sold 212,000 in the United States alone by year-end and ultimately over 9 million copies. It spawned Counter-Strike as a fan mod. Valve used the revenue to build Steam.

events.title: Halo: Combat Evolved Launches with Xbox
events.blurb: Microsoft needed a reason for anyone to buy its new video game console from a software company. A science-fiction shooter about a soldier in powered armour became that reason. It sold one million copies faster than any console game in history, perfected twin-stick controller shooting, and made Xbox Live into the template for every online console service that followed.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 2001 — Halo: Combat Evolved launched as a launch title for the original Xbox. Bungie had originally developed it as a Mac/PC real-time strategy game before Microsoft acquired the studio.

events.title: World of Warcraft Launches
events.blurb: An online game that charged a monthly subscription fee on top of a $50 box price acquired half a million players in its first week and 12 million at its peak — more than the population of several European nations. It swallowed years of people's lives, birthed the term "raiding," generated academic papers about its simulated epidemics, and made "massively multiplayer" a standard genre.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 2004 — World of Warcraft launched in North America, Australia, and New Zealand. In 2020, researchers cited WoW's 2005 "Corrupted Blood" plague — an accidental in-game epidemic — as a realistic model for studying pandemic behaviour. Lifetime revenue exceeded $9 billion.

events.title: Minecraft Officially Released
events.blurb: A game with no story, no tutorial, no win state, and graphics that looked like 1989 asked players to punch trees and build whatever they wanted. It became the best-selling video game of all time. Schools adopted it as an educational tool. A generation learned their first lessons about architecture, resource management, and server administration inside it.
events.revealBlurb: November 18, 2011 — Minecraft version 1.0.0 launched at Minecon in Las Vegas. Microsoft acquired developer Mojang in 2014 for $2.5 billion. By 2025 the game had sold over 350 million copies — more than twice the second-best-selling game.

events.title: Liverpool-Manchester Railway Opens
events.blurb: The world's first inter-city passenger railway line opened with ceremony, carrying dignitaries including the Duke of Wellington on eight parallel trains along a 56-kilometre line linking the port of Liverpool with the cotton-manufacturing centre of Manchester. A parliamentary member, William Huskisson, stepped onto the tracks at a refueling stop and was struck by an oncoming locomotive. He died that evening — the first well-known railway fatality.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1830 — designed by George Stephenson. Huskisson is universally regarded as the first prominent casualty of the railway age, though he was not strictly the first railway death. The line ran horse- and steam-hauled freight alongside passengers for its first decades.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Edison Invents Phonograph
events.blurb: A 30-year-old American inventor shouted the first verse of "Mary Had a Little Lamb" into the horn of a machine he had built at his New Jersey laboratory, then cranked a handle to make the machine play his words back to him. Recording sound — not just transmitting it instantaneously as the telephone did — had never been done before. The device, a tinfoil-cylinder phonograph, would be followed by commercial wax-cylinder versions by the end of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1877 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. The original tinfoil phonograph could replay a recording only a few times before the foil wore out. The machine astonished audiences when Edison demonstrated it at the Scientific American office a week later.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Elizabeth I Accession
events.blurb: A 25-year-old unmarried princess, the daughter of a beheaded second queen who had once been declared a bastard, became Queen of England on the death of her half-sister. She had survived imprisonment and political marginalization under her sister's Catholic restoration. Her 44-year reign would see the English settlement of Ireland, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flowering of Shakespeare, and the establishment of a Protestant national church still in existence.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1558 — Elizabeth I Tudor succeeds Mary I. She reportedly received the news sitting under an oak tree at Hatfield House. She never married, styled herself the "Virgin Queen," and died at 69. The state of Virginia — briefly colonized under her — is named for her.

events.title: Mayflower Compact Signed
events.blurb: 41 male passengers of a merchant ship that had landed at the wrong spot on the Massachusetts coast — they had intended the Hudson River — signed a short agreement on the ship to govern themselves by the will of the majority until permanent civil authority could be established. The document was pragmatic, not ideological, but became a foundational text of American self-government. The Pilgrims who signed it were fleeing religious persecution in England via the Netherlands.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 1620 (Old Style) / November 21, 1620 (New Style) — aboard the Mayflower, Cape Cod. Half the colony's 102 passengers died of scurvy and starvation the first winter. The autumn 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is the ancestor of the American Thanksgiving.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Casablanca Premieres
events.blurb: A wartime romance set in a Moroccan cafe — produced on a tight schedule with an often-improvised script — premiered at a New York theater two weeks after Allied troops actually landed in the real-life city, a coincidence that boosted interest. The film's lead actor and actress had expected it to be a forgettable assignment; its dialogue's half-dozen phrases would be quoted by a century of audiences. Neither of the two stars was anyone's first choice for their parts.
events.revealBlurb: November 26, 1942 — Hollywood Theatre, NYC. Director Michael Curtiz, stars Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman. "Here's looking at you, kid" was Bogart's improvisation. "Play it again, Sam" is never actually said in the film.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Teapot Dome: Senate Investigation Opens
events.blurb: The Senate launched its first formal investigation into the Teapot Dome oil fields that autumn, following revelations that Interior Secretary Albert Fall had secretly leased federal naval petroleum reserves in Wyoming and California to private oil companies in exchange for personal cash loans and gifts totaling roughly $400,000. Fall would become the first U.S. Cabinet member ever convicted of a crime committed while in office.
events.revealBlurb: October 1923 — Washington, D.C. The oil companies that paid the bribes — Sinclair Oil and Pan American Petroleum — were acquitted at trial; only the man who took the bribes was convicted. President Harding died of a heart attack in August 1923, before the scandal fully broke.

events.title: President Kennedy Assassinated in Dallas
events.blurb: At approximately 12:30 pm that day, President John F. Kennedy was shot in the head while riding in an open motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital at 1:00 pm. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested that afternoon; two days later, Oswald was shot and killed on live national television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby before he could stand trial.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1963 — Dallas, Texas. Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One, with a blood-spattered Jacqueline Kennedy standing beside him. The Warren Commission concluded Oswald acted alone; roughly 60% of Americans have never believed it.

events.title: Obergefell v. Hodges: Same-Sex Marriage Nationwide
events.blurb: The Supreme Court held 5–4 that the Constitution guarantees same-sex couples the right to marry, requiring all 50 states to issue marriage licenses and recognize same-sex unions performed elsewhere. Justice Anthony Kennedy's majority opinion grounded the right in both the Due Process and Equal Protection clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 2015 — Washington, D.C. The case's lead plaintiff, Jim Obergefell, had sought only to have his name listed on his deceased husband's death certificate as the surviving spouse. When the ruling was announced, the White House was illuminated in rainbow colors that night.

events.title: COVID-19 National Emergency Declared
events.blurb: President Donald Trump declared a national emergency, unlocking $50 billion in federal disaster funds to respond to the coronavirus pandemic, which had by then spread to 49 states and killed dozens of Americans. The pandemic would ultimately claim over 1.1 million American lives — more than any war in the country's history — and shut down schools, businesses, and public life for over a year.
events.revealBlurb: March 13, 2020 — The White House. The first confirmed U.S. case had been detected just 53 days earlier. Within weeks, American unemployment reached 14.7% — the highest since the Great Depression — as roughly 22 million jobs vanished in two months.

events.title: "Who Shot J.R.?" Revealed
events.blurb: An estimated 83 million American viewers — 76 percent of all active television sets at the time — tuned in to a prime-time U.S. soap opera to learn who had fired the cliffhanger-ending shot that had kept the nation guessing for eight months. At the time it was the most-watched single program in television history. Souvenir T-shirts, novelty songs, and betting pools had all sprouted during the summer hiatus between seasons.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1980 — Dallas, episode "Who Done It." The shooter was Kristin Shepard, played by Mary Crosby. J.R. Ewing survived. The "Who Shot J.R.?" plot is considered a pioneer of the season-ending cliffhanger in prime-time television.

events.title: Prince's Purple Rain Released
events.blurb: A 26-year-old Minneapolis musician released his sixth studio album — the soundtrack to a semi-autobiographical feature film he had also starred in. The album's nine tracks combined funk, rock, R&B, and gospel into a sound that critics had long despaired of finding. It sat at number one on the Billboard 200 for 24 consecutive weeks. The artist held a complex, rivalrous relationship with Michael Jackson's Thriller era.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1984 — Prince and the Revolution. The accompanying film grossed $68 million on a $7 million budget. The album's singles "When Doves Cry" and "Let's Go Crazy" both hit #1. Prince died in 2016 at 57 from an accidental fentanyl overdose.

events.title: Milli Vanilli Grammy Stripped
events.blurb: The Recording Academy revoked a Grammy award given to a German-based pop duo nine months earlier after the duo's producer, fired in a dispute, revealed publicly that the duo had not actually sung on their multi-platinum album — other studio vocalists had. The two dreadlocked frontmen had been, in effect, models who lip-synced. The scandal ended their careers; the Recording Academy has not revoked a Grammy for any reason since.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1990 — Milli Vanilli (Rob Pilatus and Fab Morvan) stripped of their 1989 Best New Artist Grammy. Rob Pilatus was found dead in 1998 at 32 of an accidental overdose. Fab Morvan has continued to perform. The actual vocalists included Charles Shaw, John Davis, and Brad Howell.

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: Seinfeld Finale
events.blurb: The 180th and final episode of a nine-year NBC sitcom about petty New York narcissists aired to 76 million viewers. The divisive finale had the four main characters put on trial in a fictional Massachusetts town for failing to help a carjacking victim, watched by a parade of minor characters from earlier seasons who had been wronged by them. Critics and fans were largely disappointed; its creator defended it as consistent with the show's amoral premise.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1998 — "The Finale." Written by Larry David, returning after leaving the show in 1996. Ad slots on the finale sold for around $2 million for 30 seconds — a pre-Super Bowl record for a TV program.

events.title: Justinian's Code Issued
events.blurb: A Byzantine emperor's commission of ten jurists, working for 14 months, compiled nearly a thousand years of Roman legal rulings into a single four-part code. It became the foundation of civil-law systems across continental Europe and, centuries later, Latin America. Imperial-era laws contradicted themselves; the code resolved the contradictions by fiat.
events.revealBlurb: April 7, 529 — Emperor Justinian I issued the first edition. The final compilation, called the Corpus Juris Civilis, influenced the Napoleonic Code and every legal system modeled on it. Law students still read excerpts today.

events.title: William the Conqueror Crowned
events.blurb: Ten weeks after winning a decisive battle on the south coast of England, the Norman duke who had invaded was crowned king at a Westminster abbey. During the coronation, Norman guards outside the abbey mistook acclamations for riot and set fire to nearby houses; the new king was hurriedly anointed while smoke drifted through the doors. He would never be popular with his new subjects.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1066 — Westminster Abbey. William spent the next two decades building castles, compiling the Domesday Book, and crushing rebellions. He was buried in Caen, and his tomb was opened, profaned, and emptied of bones during the French Revolution.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Black Death Reaches Europe
events.blurb: A plague arriving by trade galley at a Sicilian port spread through Mediterranean shipping lanes and overland caravans until, over the next five years, it killed an estimated 30-60 percent of Europe's population — perhaps 50 million people. Physicians had no effective response; flagellant processions and mass pogroms of Jews did little but spread the disease faster.
events.revealBlurb: October 1347 — Messina, Sicily. Caused by Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of black rats. Wages for surviving laborers roughly doubled; labor scarcity began eroding feudal obligations. The plague cycled back every decade or so for the next three centuries.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: Parthenon Completed
events.blurb: A marble temple dedicated to the patron goddess of an Athenian acropolis was completed after fifteen years of work. The structure refined classical Doric proportions, incorporated subtle optical corrections (all its columns lean slightly inward, curved "entasis" swelling their shafts) so the temple appears perfectly rectilinear from a distance, and housed a 12-metre ivory-and-gold statue of Athena. It stood substantially intact for over 2,000 years until a Venetian shell hit a Turkish powder magazine inside it in 1687.
events.revealBlurb: 438 BCE — Ictinus and Callicrates, architects, under Phidias as sculptor. Built on the acropolis of Athens under Pericles. The Elgin Marbles, sold to the British Museum in 1816, are fragments of the Parthenon's sculptural programme — still the subject of Greek repatriation demands.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years.
