The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: Versailles Hall of Mirrors Completed
events.blurb: A French king's chief architect and royal painter completed the centerpiece of a vastly enlarged royal palace on the edge of Paris — a 73-metre-long gallery of 578 mirror panels on one side, facing 17 tall windows overlooking the palace gardens on the other, with a vaulted ceiling painted with 30 scenes of the king's military triumphs. Mirrors were at the time so expensive that a single pane could cost as much as a small estate; the gallery was a showcase of French glassmaking independence from Venice.
events.revealBlurb: 1684 — Jules Hardouin-Mansart (architect) and Charles Le Brun (painter) for Louis XIV. The Treaty of Versailles ending WWI was signed in the room on June 28, 1919 — a deliberate German humiliation in the same space where German unification had been proclaimed in 1871.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: Pokémon GO Launches
events.blurb: A mobile game using GPS and augmented reality sent tens of millions of people into parks, cemeteries, and government buildings to catch fictional creatures on their phones. It broke multiple App Store records in its first 24 hours. Police stations issued public statements asking players not to enter. Central Park held impromptu gatherings of thousands at midnight.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Pokémon GO launched in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand. It surpassed 100 million downloads in under 30 days and generated $207 million in its first month — the highest ever for a mobile game. Lifetime revenue has surpassed $6 billion.

events.title: Bob Marley's Exodus Released
events.blurb: A Jamaican reggae star, recovering in a London flat after being shot in an assassination attempt at his home five months earlier, released his ninth studio album. Its tracks — "Three Little Birds," "One Love," "Jamming," "Waiting in Vain," and the title track — would become the core of his international legacy. Time magazine named it the album of the century. He had fled to London for his safety; the exile shaped the record.
events.revealBlurb: June 3, 1977 — Bob Marley and the Wailers. The album was recorded at Island Studios in London. The attempted assassination on December 3, 1976 had injured him, his wife, and his manager. Marley would die of cancer at 36 in 1981.

events.title: Thriller Released
events.blurb: A 24-year-old singer released his sixth studio album, a collection of nine tracks deliberately designed so every one could be a single. The 14-minute title track's horror-film music video, featuring choreographed zombie dancing, premiered the following December on a cable channel that had until recently been reluctant to play Black artists. The album became, and remains, the best-selling album of all time.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1982 — Michael Jackson, produced by Quincy Jones. It has sold over 70 million copies worldwide. The moonwalk, which Jackson debuted performing "Billie Jean" at Motown's 25th-anniversary TV special 3.5 months after release, was not actually his invention.

events.title: Paul Simon's Graceland Released
events.blurb: A 44-year-old American songwriter released an album recorded largely in Johannesburg studios with South African musicians, fusing American folk and pop with mbaqanga, isicathamiya, and zydeco. The album was controversial: the United Nations had called for a cultural boycott of the apartheid regime, and many considered the recording sessions a violation. The finished record was nonetheless a critical and commercial phenomenon and was credited with exposing mass audiences to South African musical traditions.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1986 — Paul Simon. Collaborators included Ladysmith Black Mambazo, Ray Phiri, and the Boyoyo Boys. Simon was blacklisted by the UN but sang in Zimbabwe and Zambia; Nelson Mandela later thanked him for the cultural bridge.

events.title: Freddie Mercury Dies
events.blurb: A 45-year-old rock singer issued a statement from his London home the previous day confirming the rumors he had been fighting for years: he had AIDS. He died the next evening of bronchial pneumonia resulting from the disease. His band's 1975 operatic epic had just re-entered the UK charts on the back of its use in a film released the previous May, and climbed to number one the week after he died.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1991 — Freddie Mercury of Queen. The film was "Wayne's World"; the song "Bohemian Rhapsody." A tribute concert at Wembley Stadium the following April was broadcast to over a billion people.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Operation Barbarossa
events.blurb: Three million soldiers, 600,000 motorised vehicles, 3,600 tanks, and 2,700 aircraft crossed a 2,900-kilometre border in the pre-dawn darkness, launching the largest land invasion in military history. The defender's air force lost over a thousand planes in the first day, many of them still on the ground.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1941. Stalin reportedly refused to believe his own border commanders' early reports and assumed the attacks were unauthorised provocations. The operation's codename referenced the medieval Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. By December, Germany had advanced 1,000 km but failed to knock the Soviet Union out of the war.

events.title: First Nuclear Chain Reaction
events.blurb: In a squash court beneath a university stadium, a team of physicists assembled 45,000 carefully machined blocks of graphite around pellets of uranium into a lattice the size of a house, withdrew a control rod, and achieved humanity's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — completing the key step toward a new category of weapon.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1942, under Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. Enrico Fermi's team celebrated with a bottle of Chianti in paper cups. The coded telegram sent to Washington read: "The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World." The reactor sat in a populated neighbourhood with no containment vessel.

events.title: Tehran Conference
events.blurb: The three most powerful leaders of the opposing alliance met for the first time in a capital city in southwest Asia, committing to a firm timeline for a massive cross-channel invasion in spring, agreeing on the postwar borders of one eastern European nation, and beginning to sketch the political shape of the world that would follow the conflict.
events.revealBlurb: November 28 – December 1, 1943 — FDR, Churchill, and Stalin met in Tehran. It was the first time FDR and Stalin met in person. Roosevelt, whose security staff feared assassination, moved into the Soviet Embassy at Stalin's suggestion — and Soviet intelligence promptly bugged his suite. Churchill celebrated his 69th birthday at the conference with a dinner attended by all three leaders.

events.title: Yalta Conference
events.blurb: Three heads of government convened at a palatial Crimean resort to decide the political geography of the postwar world — agreeing on the division of a defeated nation into occupation zones, the formation of a new international peace organisation, and the borders of several countries whose populations had no vote in the matter.
events.revealBlurb: February 4–11, 1945. FDR was visibly ill — he would be dead in two months — and Soviet diplomats exploited his eagerness for a deal. Stalin's concessions on free elections in Eastern Europe proved worthless within two years. Churchill reportedly told his doctor: "I do not suppose that at any moment in history has the agony of the world been so great or widespread."

events.title: Indian National Congress Founded
events.blurb: Seventy-two delegates — mostly English-educated Indian lawyers, journalists, and teachers, along with a few sympathetic Britons — met at a college in a western Indian port city for a three-day conference to petition the colonial government for greater Indian representation in its administration. The polite gathering would, over six decades, become the vehicle of a mass independence movement.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1885 — Bombay (now Mumbai). The prime mover was a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume, who believed organized political expression would prevent revolution. He was half right.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Operation Blue Star
events.blurb: The Indian Army was ordered to storm the holiest shrine of the Sikh religion, in a Punjabi city, to dislodge a militant preacher and a few hundred armed followers who had fortified the temple complex. The operation, fought with tanks and artillery inside the precinct, killed the militant leader, at least 83 soldiers, and several hundred pilgrims and militants. It traumatized the Sikh community and set in motion events that would kill the prime minister who had ordered it.
events.revealBlurb: June 1-8, 1984 — the target was Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale at the Golden Temple, Amritsar. Four months and three weeks later, Indira Gandhi was assassinated by two of her own Sikh bodyguards.

events.title: Kargil War
events.blurb: Pakistani soldiers, disguised as local insurgents, occupied high-altitude ridges inside the Indian-administered portion of a disputed northern territory over the winter. Their discovery by a shepherd in early May touched off a 74-day war fought at elevations up to 5,600 metres. India retook the peaks one by one with heavy infantry losses; Pakistan, pressured by Washington, withdrew.
events.revealBlurb: May 3 to July 26, 1999 — the Line of Control in Kargil, Ladakh. The conflict was one of the first televised wars in India. Captain Vikram Batra became a national hero before dying on Point 4875 on July 7.

events.title: 26/11 Mumbai Attacks
events.blurb: Ten men trained by a Pakistan-based militant group landed at a fishing harbour in the country's financial capital by rubber dinghy after hijacking an Indian fishing trawler at sea, and fanned out across the city to attack a railway station, a Jewish centre, a café, and two luxury hotels. The resulting sieges lasted 60 hours. 166 people died and more than 300 were wounded. Nine attackers were killed; the sole survivor was captured, tried, and hanged four years later.
events.revealBlurb: November 26-29, 2008 — Mumbai. The captured gunman, Ajmal Kasab, was hanged on November 21, 2012. The attacks were coordinated over satellite phone from Karachi; the operational planner, Sajid Mir, was finally convicted in Pakistan in 2022.

events.title: Galileo Maps the Moon
events.blurb: An Italian natural philosopher directed a 20× magnification tube skyward and produced detailed drawings of the Moon's surface, revealing mountains and craters rather than a perfect celestial sphere as ancient philosophy held. He calculated the heights of lunar mountains by measuring the lengths of the shadows they cast.

events.title: Galileo Observes the Moon Through a Telescope
events.blurb: Turning a new optical instrument toward the night sky, an Italian mathematician observed that the Moon's surface was rough, mountainous, and marked by craters — directly contradicting the ancient belief that celestial bodies were perfect smooth spheres. Careful drawings of the shadow lines allowed him to estimate the height of lunar mountains by triangulating shadow lengths.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1609 — Galileo had only heard a description of a Dutch spyglass and built his own without ever seeing one. His 1610 pamphlet Sidereus Nuncius went through its entire print run within a week. He dedicated Jupiter's four moons to the Medici family to secure patronage — an early example of branded science.

events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: Radioactivity Discovered
events.blurb: A French physicist studying uranium salts placed a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer alongside a uranium sample during several cloudy days, expecting to run a sunlight experiment later. When he developed the plate anyway, he found a sharp image — proving the uranium was spontaneously emitting invisible radiation with no external energy source, a phenomenon no existing theory could explain.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1896 — Henri Becquerel announced to the Academy of Sciences that the image was "very distinct." The discovery was accidental: bad weather cancelled his planned sunlight experiment. He initially thought it was a variant of X-rays; it took the Curies to show radioactivity was a property of the atom itself.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: Wikipedia Launched
events.blurb: A 34-year-old internet entrepreneur who had been trying to build an online encyclopedia by paying credentialed experts to write and peer-review articles gave up on the slow model and switched to a radical alternative: a wiki, editable by anyone. The new version grew faster than expected. It had more articles in its first year than the slow-model version had produced in a previous eighteen months.
events.revealBlurb: January 15, 2001 — Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. By 2007 Wikipedia had surpassed Britannica in size and approximately in accuracy. Today's English Wikipedia has over 6.9 million articles, and the full project runs in 340+ languages.

events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: WikiLeaks Cablegate
events.blurb: A whistleblower-platform website and a consortium of five newspapers began publishing, in coordinated waves, 251,287 U.S. diplomatic cables leaked by a 22-year-old U.S. Army intelligence analyst. The cables ranged from the mundane to the explosive — unflattering private assessments of world leaders, evidence of corruption in allied governments, and revelations about civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan. The leaker would face the longest sentence ever imposed for leaking U.S. government information.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 2010 — leaker Chelsea Manning (then Bradley), sentenced to 35 years in 2013. Obama commuted her sentence in 2017. WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange lived in the Ecuadorian embassy in London from 2012 until 2019; he was released from UK custody in a 2024 plea deal.

events.title: ChatGPT Launched
events.blurb: A San Francisco AI research lab released, as an unassuming "research preview," a conversational interface to its large language model. The chatbot could answer questions, write essays, debug code, and generate poetry in response to natural-language prompts. It gained a hundred million monthly users within two months — making it the fastest-growing consumer product in history. Incumbent tech giants pivoted their entire product strategies within weeks.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 2022 — OpenAI. The underlying model, GPT-3.5, had existed for months; the chat wrapper made all the difference. By 2025, generative AI had become a ~$200 billion global industry. Anthropic, Google, Meta, and xAI joined OpenAI as frontier labs.

events.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: The first of three Reconstruction-era amendments was ratified eight months after a brutal civil war ended, abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States except as punishment for crime. The exception clause would become the legal scaffolding for convict-leasing systems that reproduced plantation labor for another 80 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1865 — when Georgia became the 27th state to ratify. Mississippi officially ratified only in 1995, and didn't certify it until 2013, due to a paperwork oversight.

events.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Ratified in the aftermath of civil war, a constitutional amendment granted citizenship to "all persons born or naturalized in the United States," promised them equal protection under the laws, and guaranteed due process. Its sweeping language became, a century later, the foundation of Supreme Court rulings on school segregation, interracial marriage, abortion, and marriage equality.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1868 — citizenship via birthright. Its authors were thinking of formerly enslaved people; its practical effect reshaped virtually every area of American law. The "equal protection clause" alone has been cited in over 400 Supreme Court cases.

events.title: Rosa Parks Arrested
events.blurb: A 42-year-old department-store seamstress and longtime NAACP secretary refused to give up her seat on a city bus in an Alabama capital when the white section filled up and the driver demanded the first row of Black seating. She was arrested for violating municipal segregation ordinances. The local Black community organized a one-day bus boycott that became a 381-day boycott.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1955 — Montgomery, Alabama. Parks was not, as legend has it, "too tired" to move — she was a trained activist who had attended a civil rights training school months earlier. Her act was calculated. A 26-year-old new preacher in town, Martin Luther King Jr., was chosen to lead the boycott.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Freedom Summer Murders
events.blurb: Three voter-registration volunteers — two Jewish New Yorkers and a local Black civil rights worker — disappeared after being arrested for an alleged traffic violation, released at night, and abducted by Klansmen near a Mississippi town. Their bodies were found 44 days later, bulldozed into an earthen dam. A massive FBI manhunt — the first major civil rights intervention by the Bureau — cracked the case.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1964 — Philadelphia, Mississippi. James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner. The state refused to prosecute; federal civil-rights conspiracy charges netted seven convictions. The ringleader, Edgar Ray Killen, was finally convicted of manslaughter in 2005 at age 80.

events.title: Thriller Album Released
events.blurb: A recording artist released a 42-minute album featuring nine tracks, seven of which became top-ten singles on the Billboard Hot 100 — a chart achievement never matched before or since. The album sold more than 66 million copies, and its 14-minute title-track music video transformed the medium from a promotional clip into an art form.

events.title: Ghostbusters Released
events.blurb: A comedy directed by and starring several members of a Saturday Night Live cast followed a team of parapsychology PhDs turned paranormal exterminators in New York City. The film grossed $282 million on a $30 million budget and became the highest-grossing comedy to that point. Its theme song, written under deadline pressure, sat at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 for three weeks. A marshmallow man the size of a skyscraper became the film's most memorable villain.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1984 — Ivan Reitman directing Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Harold Ramis, and Ernie Hudson. Theme song by Ray Parker Jr. The marshmallow costume, worn by actor William Atherton, weighed 45 kg and caused heat exhaustion.

events.title: We Are the World Recorded
events.blurb: Forty-five American pop stars gathered at a Los Angeles recording studio after the annual American Music Awards ceremony to record a charity single for African famine relief, written by two headliners in a single evening. The recording session ran until 8 AM. The single sold over 20 million copies and raised more than $63 million. Its producer had hung a sign at the studio entrance reading: "Check your ego at the door."
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1985 — written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie; produced by Quincy Jones. Participating artists included Stevie Wonder, Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan, Diana Ross, and Ray Charles. The sign was Jones's idea. A 2024 Netflix documentary rehashed the making of the track.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Tamagotchi Released
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company released a small egg-shaped plastic keychain with a tiny LCD screen and three buttons. The device simulated a virtual pet that needed feeding, playing with, and cleaning up after — with beeps demanding attention at all hours, including in the middle of lessons in schools. Schools banned them. 40 million units sold globally. The craze prefigured the attention-hijacking mobile apps of decades later.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 1996 — Bandai. Designed by Akihiro Yokoi and Aki Maita. Later versions could be put to sleep or paused; the original would simply "die" if neglected, and the keychain had to be reset. The name combines Japanese "tamago" (egg) and "watch."
